title: Testing and Debugging Automations
summary: An automation that works once on perfect data is not finished - a professional tests and debugs thoroughly so it works on the messy reality of production, and this discipline prevents costly mistakes. Testing starts with running your workflow on samp
content:
# Testing and Debugging Automations ##### "But it worked when I tested it" A freelancer delivered an invoice automation to a client: form submission in, invoice PDF out, emailed to the customer, logged to a sheet. She tested it four times with her own details. Perfect every time. Week one in production produced: an invoice addressed to "" because someone left the company field blank; a ₹0 invoice because a price arrived as `"1,299"` and the number conversion returned `NaN`; two identical invoices for one order because the client double-clicked Submit; and a run that crashed entirely on a customer named `O'Brien` because of an unescaped apostrophe. None of those inputs were exotic. They were simply *not the input she tested with*. She had tested that the automation could succeed. She had never tested whether it could fail. Andreas Zeller's book on systematic debugging makes the point that debugging is a science, not a guessing game — you form a hypothesis, test it, and narrow the search. Today you learn both halves: how to test automations deliberately, and how to debug them systematically rather than by poking. ##### Testing with sample and edge-case data Professional testing means deliberately constructing inputs designed to break your workflow. Work through this checklist for every automation you build. **Missing data** - A required field absent entirely (the key is not in the payload). - A field present but empty (`""`). - A field present but `null`. - An array with zero elements. These four are genuinely different, and workflows routinely handle one and crash on the others. **Wrong types and formats** - A number arriving as text: `"45"`, or worse, `"45 people"`. - A date in an unexpected format: `05/01/2024`, `Jan 5 2024`, `2024-1-5`. - A currency string: `"₹1,299.00"`. - A boolean as the string `"false"` — which is truthy in most languages. **Boundary values** - Zero, negative numbers, very large numbers. - Exactly the threshold your filter tests (if the rule is "over 50," test 49, 50 and 51). - An empty list and a list of 500 items. - A very long string in a field with a length limit. **Awkward characters** - Apostrophes: `O'Brien`, `D'Souza`. - Non-ASCII: `Prajñā`, `ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು`, `₹`, emoji. - Leading/trailing whitespace: `" ananya@example.com "`. - HTML or SQL fragments in a text field. **Duplicates and repeats** - The same record submitted twice. - The same webhook delivered twice (retries do this). - Re-running the whole workflow on data it already processed. **Failure conditions** - An expired credential. - An unreachable endpoint (point a URL at something invalid). - A rate limit (fire many requests quickly). - A timeout (a very large payload). Write these as a **test plan table** before you start: ```text # | Case | Input | Expected --|-------------------------|------------------------------|---------------------------- 1 | Happy path | full valid record | row created, email sent 2 | Missing email | email key absent | skipped, logged, no email 3 | Empty company | company = "" | defaults to "Unknown" 4 | Price as text w/ symbol | "₹1,299.00" | stored as 1299.00 5 | Duplicate submit | same order_id twice | exactly one row exists 6 | Apostrophe in name | "Rhea D'Souza" | stored intact, no crash 7 | Boundary team size | 49 / 50 / 51 | small / small / enterprise 8 | Dead endpoint | invalid API URL | 3 retries, then alert ``` A table like this, filled in with actual results, is exactly the mini project deliverable — and it is a genuinely impressive artefact to show an interviewer, because almost no junior candidate produces one. ##### Reading run history and execution logs Every platform records what happened. Learning to read those records fluently is the highest-leverage debugging skill you can develop. **Zapier — Task History.** Every run, with status: *Success*, *Filtered* (a filter stopped it — not an error), *Held*, *Stopped*, *Errored*. Open a run and each step shows a **Data In** and **Data Out** panel containing the exact JSON. Filter the history by Zap, status and date to find the failing runs quickly. **Make.com — History tab and execution bubbles.** Each execution shows every module with its input and output **bundles**, plus the operations consumed. Turn on *Allow storing of Incomplete Executions* so failed runs are parked for inspection and manual retry rather than vanishing. **n8n — Executions list.** The richest view: open any past execution and you see the whole canvas frozen in that run's state, with every node's INPUT and OUTPUT inspectable in Table, JSON or Schema view. You can even copy a failed execution's data back into the editor to reproduce it. The universal technique: **compare what you expected the data to be with what it actually was, one step at a time.** Nearly every bug is visible the moment you look at the right step's actual data. ##### Debugging step by step Here is the systematic process — and this is what the assignment asks you to describe. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Automation failed] --> B[Read the error message
fully and literally] B --> C[Open the failed run
in run history] C --> D[Find the FIRST failing step
not the last one] D --> E[Inspect that step's INPUT
is the data what you expected?] E -->|input is wrong| F[The bug is UPSTREAM
move one step back] F --> E E -->|input is right| G[The bug is in THIS step
config, mapping, or the API] G --> H[Form one hypothesis] H --> I[Change ONE thing
and re-run] I --> J{Fixed?} J -->|no| H J -->|yes| K[Add a test case for it
then re-run the full suite] ``` The steps in words: 1. **Read the error literally.** `Cannot read property 'email' of undefined` means something you expected to be an object was not there. `422 Unprocessable Entity` means the API received your request and rejected the contents — the response body usually says which field. 2. **Reproduce it.** A bug you cannot reproduce cannot be confirmed fixed. Capture the exact input that failed and re-run with it. 3. **Find the first failing step.** Later errors are usually consequences. Fix the earliest one. 4. **Compare expected vs actual input** at that step. This single comparison resolves the majority of bugs. 5. **Bisect.** If the workflow is long, check the middle: is the data still correct there? That halves your search space each time. 6. **Change one thing at a time.** Changing three things and seeing it work teaches you nothing about which mattered. 7. **Add a test case** for the bug so it cannot silently return. Two tools worth adding to workflows deliberately: a **logging step** that writes each run's key values to a sheet or table, and a **no-op / Set node** placed mid-workflow purely to snapshot the data at that point. Both cost little and save hours. ##### Test versus production environments Testing against live systems is how people learn this lesson the hard way — by emailing 400 real customers a test message, or creating 60 junk records in a client's CRM. Separate your environments: | | Test | Production | |---|---|---| | Data | Fake records, your own email | Real customers | | Credentials | Sandbox/test API keys | Live keys | | Destinations | Test sheet, `#bot-testing` channel | Real sheet, real channels | | Volume | A handful of records | Full traffic | | Blast radius | Zero | Real money and reputation | Practical ways to achieve this without much effort: - **Duplicate the workflow** and name it `[TEST] Order sync`, pointed at test destinations. - **Use sandbox credentials.** Stripe, Razorpay, HubSpot and most serious APIs provide them free. - **Add a kill switch:** an early filter `if ENV != "prod" then only continue for emails ending in @yourdomain.com`. - **Use separate n8n instances or Make folders** for dev and prod. - **Never point a test run at a live send.** If you must test email, send to yourself or a mail-catching service like Mailtrap. An example of what goes wrong without separation: a student testing a "notify all customers of order status" workflow with the live customer table and a live email connection. One click, 1,200 emails, including several saying `Hi undefined, your order test123 has shipped`. The client noticed. ##### Common failure patterns and their fixes | Symptom | Usual cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | Field is blank downstream | Wrong mapping, or optional field absent | Check the step's Data Out; use a default | | `401` / `403` | Expired or under-scoped credential | Reconnect; check scopes | | `404` | Wrong URL, or record deleted | Verify endpoint and ID | | `422` / `400` | Payload shape or types wrong | Read the response body; check required fields | | `429` | Rate limit | Add delay, batch, back off | | Only the first item processed | An array without an iterator | Add Iterator / Split Out / Loop | | Duplicates appearing | No idempotency check | Search-then-update, or a unique constraint | | Works sometimes | Race condition, timing, or inconsistent input | Add waits/retries; test with varied data | | Runs but does nothing | Filter is stopping it | Check for *Filtered* status in history | | Wrong times | Time zone not set | Pin the time zone everywhere | | Infinite loop | Workflow writes to its own trigger source | Break the cycle or add a source marker | ##### Common pitfalls in testing itself - **Testing only the happy path.** - **Testing with your own perfectly formatted data** — real users are messier than you. - **Not testing failure modes** — if you have never seen your error handler fire, it does not work. - **Fixing symptoms rather than causes** — patching a blank field downstream instead of finding why it is blank. - **Changing several things at once.** - **Not re-testing after a fix** — regressions are real. - **No documentation of what was tested**, so nobody knows the coverage. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: take one of your automations and test it against **at least four edge cases** — missing field, empty input, duplicate, odd format — using the run history to inspect **each step**, and fix what you find. Expect to find something. Every automation built without edge-case testing has at least one of these bugs; discovering yours is the point. The mini project turns that into a professional artefact: a **documented test plan** listing normal and edge-case inputs, expected outputs and actual results; run each, capture run-history evidence (screenshots of the failing step's data are ideal), and record the fixes you made to reach a fully passing state. Present it as a table like the one above. For the assignment, describe your **step-by-step debugging process** — read the error, reproduce, find the first failing step, compare expected vs actual input, bisect, change one thing, add a regression test — and explain **why a test environment matters** with a concrete example of what goes wrong without one. The 1,200-emails story, or an equivalent from your own testing, makes the argument far better than an abstract statement. ##### Key takeaways - Test deliberately for missing fields, wrong types, boundaries, awkward characters, duplicates and failure conditions — not just the happy path. - Run history is your debugger: compare each step's actual input and output against what you expected. - Debug systematically — find the *first* failing step, form one hypothesis, change one thing, then add a regression test. - Separate test from production with duplicate workflows, sandbox credentials, test destinations and a kill-switch filter. - Learn the common failure patterns; most production incidents are a mapping error, a missing iterator, an expired credential, a rate limit, or a missing idempotency check.
